title: Bug or Feature$^2$: Weight Drift and Activation Sparsity
claim: A feedback loop between loss gradients and weights self-reinforces a bias, driving a systematic shift that yields sparsity.
layout: 4 boxes in a circular loop, clockwise arrows, weight-distribution inset in center
description: A circular diagram with four rounded, color-coded boxes connected by thick black clockwise arrows. At the top is a green box, 'Activations: ReLU(p) ≥ 0'. An arrow labeled 'loss (MSE, Cross Entropy)' leads right to a red box, 'Gradients: E[∂ℓ/∂p] ≥ 0'. A second arrow, labeled '−η∇_w ℓ', leads to a blue box at the bottom, 'Weights: E[w] < 0'. An arrow labeled 'p = Wh' leads left to a purple box, 'Pre-activations: E[p] < 0'. A final arrow labeled 'ReLU' returns to the green box. In the center is a small inset: a blue Gaussian density over w with a dashed zero line. A faded dashed copy of the curve sits to the right, and a blue arrow points left to show the shift toward negative values. The eye goes first to the colored boxes, then follows the loop.
caption: Negative weight drift is a self-reinforcing loop. Under MSE or cross-entropy loss, ReLU activations make the expected gradient with respect to pre-activations non-negative (§2). Gradient descent therefore shifts the weight distribution toward negative values (inset), which pushes pre-activations below zero and closes the loop. ReLU maps the shifted pre-activations to zero, producing activation sparsity (§4–§5).
abstract: The design of modern neural architectures has converged through incremental empirical choices, yet the mechanisms governing their training dynamics remain only partially understood. We identify and analyze a negative weight drift induced by the interaction between standard losses and positively biased activation functions. We prove that under MSE or cross-entropy loss, the gradient with respect to positive pre-activations is non-negative in expectation at initialization, driving downstream weights toward negative values during early training. The drift is intrinsic to optimization rather than data, and persists across architectures and asymmetric activation functions (ReLU, GELU, SiLU). Coupled with ReLU, weight drift produces activation sparsity reaching nearly 90% in GPT-nano. We further analyze whether this natural sparsity is damaging and find that, on average, models sharply degrade above $\sim$70% activation sparsity. We then evaluate sparsity-inducing activation functions, which reveals activation spikes in intermediate transformer layers. Code is available at https://github.com/On-Point-RND/BugOrFeature.
